summaries.example: Imagine a word such as “animal.” Wyclif thought a general word like this points to a real common nature shared by many individual animals, not merely to an idea in someone’s mind. He also thought careful attention to words could help us understand how the world is put together.
summaries.summary: John Wyclif was an important fourteenth-century English thinker. He worked at Oxford, wrote in Latin and English, and became both a philosopher and a religious reformer. His philosophy was built around the idea that reality, thought, and language fit together. He believed that general kinds, called universals, are real features shared by individual things. Because he trusted this view, he treated logic and language as ways of describing the world’s real structure. Wyclif also wrote about being, truth, God, the Church, the Bible, and ownership. He taught that the Bible has complete authority and criticized church wealth and power. His unusual views about the Eucharist and other religious doctrines led to condemnation. His writings influenced later thinkers and reform movements, even though some parts of his system were unclear or difficult to make consistent.
key_ideas: John Wyclif was a major English philosopher and religious reformer of the later Middle Ages.
He believed that language should match the structure of reality as closely as possible.
He argued that universals, such as human nature, are real and are connected with individual things.
His ideas about words, truth, being, and religion were closely connected.
He criticized the wealth and authority of parts of the medieval Church and gave Scripture a very high place.
Some of his views about the Church, the Eucharist, God’s power, and human freedom were condemned by church authorities.
summaries.why_it_matters: Wyclif shows how one person’s ideas about words and reality can affect religion, society, and government. His work also helps us see why people in the Middle Ages argued about general ideas, the authority of the Church, and the meaning of truth. Studying him encourages us to ask how beliefs in one area can shape beliefs in many others.

important_terms.definition: A person who thinks general kinds, such as “human” or “animal,” have a real basis outside the mind.
A general kind or nature that can belong to many individual things.
The study of what exists and what reality is like.
A way of asking what a word stands for in a sentence.
A person who tries to change religious teaching or practice.

questions_to_think_about: Can a general word point to something real, or is it only an idea in our minds?
Why might someone think that words should match the world?
Should religious leaders be obeyed when their actions seem to conflict with sacred texts?
What problems could arise if people cannot know who has God’s special approval?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “Every human is mortal.” A nominalist might explain “human” as a useful general word for individual people. Wyclif’s realism instead treats human nature as something real outside the mind and shared by individuals. That commitment affects how he understands predication: a sentence does not merely place an object inside a class; it can express different kinds of identity or connection between metaphysical components.
summaries.summary: John Wyclif (c. 1331–1384) was a leading English philosopher of late Scholasticism and a religious reformer whose work helped prepare the intellectual climate of the Reformation. His central philosophical commitment is a robust form of realism: universals are real natures present in individuals, not merely concepts or names. He therefore seeks a close structural correspondence between language, thought, and the world. This commitment shapes his logic. His theory of supposition explains how terms stand for universals, individuals, or themselves in propositions, while his account of predication distinguishes several ways in which subject and predicate may be related. He also develops a theory of formal distinction to describe different aspects of one reality. In metaphysics, Wyclif treats being as closely connected with truth and analyzes creatures through levels of being, essence, form, and actuality. In theology, his account of divine ideas makes creation and the history of the world appear necessary, creating tension with contingency and freedom. He rejects divine annihilation and denies transubstantiation as traditionally formulated, holding that bread remains present with Christ’s body. In religious reform, he gives Scripture supreme authority, questions the standing of the visible Church, and interprets dominion as a form of stewardship dependent on divine grace. The entry emphasizes both the originality of this system and its unresolved tensions.
key_ideas: Wyclif’s philosophy combines strong realism with an insistence that language mirrors the structure of being.
He treats universals as real natures shared by individuals, while also distinguishing universal and individual aspects formally.
His account of predication includes formal, essential, and habitudinal forms, each expressing a different relation between subject and predicate.
His theory of supposition connects the meaning and truth of terms with the realities they signify, not merely with mental or linguistic conventions.
His metaphysics identifies being closely with truth and gives creatures several levels of being grounded ultimately in God.
His theology produces difficult consequences concerning divine necessity, omnipotence, the Eucharist, and human freedom; the source notes that some of these arguments do not succeed fully.
summaries.why_it_matters: Wyclif is important because his logic, metaphysics, and theology form one interconnected project. His realism influenced later Oxford thinkers, while his criticism of ecclesiastical wealth and authority influenced later religious reformers. His work also illustrates a recurring philosophical challenge: a theory can explain several problems powerfully while generating new difficulties when its basic principles are applied across logic, metaphysics, theology, and politics.

important_terms.definition: The medieval debate about whether general kinds, such as species and genera, exist outside the mind.
The view that universals have real extra-mental status, rather than being only names or mental concepts.
A distinction between entities that are genuinely different and aspects that are distinct within one reality.
Wyclif’s account of how a term stands for something in relation to its role in a proposition.
A theory that treats a proposition’s truth and meaning as grounded in what it signifies in reality.
A relation in which something is shared by different things to different degrees rather than in exactly the same way.
The medieval doctrine that bread’s substance becomes Christ’s body while its accidents remain.
Lordship or rightful authority over people or possessions, understood by Wyclif through religious ideas about grace.

questions_to_think_about: Does treating universals as real solve the problem of how one word can apply to many individuals, or create new puzzles?
What is gained by distinguishing different kinds of predication rather than giving one general account of “is”?
Can Wyclif consistently maintain both divine foreknowledge and genuine human freedom?
How does his theory of dominion turn political questions into questions about grace and religious authority?
What might be the strengths and weaknesses of grounding semantic theory in ontology?

summaries.example: Think about the word “team.” It can mean one particular team, such as your school’s team, or the general kind shared by many teams. Wyclif would ask what makes the general idea possible. He believed that general natures are real, so a common word can refer to something shared by individual things. This helped him explain why one word can apply to many things without becoming meaningless.
summaries.summary: John Wyclif was a major English thinker of the later Middle Ages. He spent much of his career at Oxford and wrote a large number of works in Latin and English. He is remembered both for his philosophy and for his criticism of the medieval Church. Wyclif’s philosophy begins with realism. He held that general natures, such as human nature, are real outside the mind and are shared by individual people. This view led him to argue that language can describe reality because words are connected with real structures. His theories of predication and supposition explain different ways that terms can stand for universals, individuals, or other expressions in sentences. He also used formal distinctions to describe how one thing can contain different aspects. Wyclif’s metaphysics and theology are closely joined. He claimed that being and truth are deeply connected, and he gave God a central role in the being of creatures. His account of divine ideas made it difficult to explain how events could be genuinely contingent or how human beings could be free. He also rejected traditional transubstantiation and held that the bread remains present with Christ’s body. As a reformer, he treated Scripture as the highest authority, criticized clerical wealth, and described dominion as a stewardship dependent on grace. Church authorities condemned some of his views, and his writings influenced later religious dissenters.
key_ideas: Wyclif was an English philosopher, teacher, and religious reformer who lived in the fourteenth century.
He opposed the idea that language and thought are only loose labels for a world that has a completely different structure.
His realism says that common natures are real and are present in individual things.
He developed detailed theories about how sentences work and how words can refer to different kinds of things.
He connected philosophy with theology, especially questions about God, creation, truth, the Bible, and the Eucharist.
He argued that Church authority should be judged by faithfulness to Scripture and that worldly power should serve a religious purpose.
summaries.why_it_matters: Wyclif matters because he shows how philosophical questions can connect with religious and social questions. His ideas about universals affected his theories of language and truth. His ideas about Scripture, Church authority, and dominion affected his view of reform. Studying him also helps us understand why medieval thinkers disagreed about reality, God’s power, human freedom, and the proper role of institutions.

important_terms.definition: The question of whether general kinds, such as “animal” or “human,” are real or only names and ideas.
The belief that general kinds have a real existence outside the mind.
A philosophical study of what exists and how different kinds of things are related.
A rule for what a word stands for when it appears in a particular sentence.
One of several ways a subject and predicate can be connected in a claim.
A difference between aspects of one thing that are not simply separate objects.
Authority or ownership understood as a responsibility given under God’s law and grace.

questions_to_think_about: If two things are both dogs, what, if anything, do they share besides a name?
Why might a philosopher think that the structure of language should resemble the structure of reality?
Can a sentence be true in more than one sense?
What should happen when a religious institution’s authority seems to conflict with Scripture?
Why would ideas about God and creation affect ideas about ownership and government?
